newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers give Belgian EMU plan good marks.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers give Belgian EMU plan good marks.

text.p: Belgium's efforts to get its budget in order for economic and monetary union (EMU) won a seal of approval from its European Union partners on Monday.

European Union finance ministers said a plan to reduce further the Belgian budget deficit and debt mountain by 2000 would add to considerable progress already made in meeting the Maastricht Treaty criteria.
"The council carried out an examination of the new Belgian convergence programme for the period 1997-2000," the ministers said in a statement.

"It welcomed the programme's strategy for budgetary consolidation as credible, adequate to the particular public finance conditions of Belgium," they said after a regular monthly meeting of their ECOFIN council.

The plan aims to cut the state deficit from 3.4 percent in 1996 to 2.9 percent in 1997 and 1.4 percent in the year 2000 in the most cautious of three economic scenarios. The ratio of debt to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is targeted to fall from 130.4 percent in 1996 to 127.0 percent in 1997 and 120.4 pct in 2000.
Belgian policies from 1992 to 1996 had led to considerable progress towards meeting the EMU criteria, the ministers said.

But they also urged Belgium to make maximum progress in cutting its debt to GDP ratio. Despite the improvement of the past few years, Belgium's debt/GDP ratio is still the worst in the 15-nation bloc.
Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told the council that Belgium's ratio of state debt to GDP was set to fall by six to 10 percentage points between 1998 and 2000.
The Maastricht Treaty on EMU sets a goal of 60 percent for the debt/GDP ratio. Higher ratios might be allowed provided there is a decline to that level "at a satisfactory pace".
Maystadt said that he expected Belgium to be among the first group of countries to join the single currency in 1999.
He said his European colleagues had expressed some worries about an overshoot in Belgian health spending, but promised that his government would keep spending in check.

"There has been a decision to put the health sector under permanent monitoring. The government will make an evaluation of the situation in the sector every month and will take the necessary measures to meet the (budgetary) norms of the government agreement," he said.
At the end of last year, Belgium took an extra 20 billion Belgian francs ($573 million) of austerity measures in the health sector following reports of a budget overshoot.

Maystadt also said that a series of scandals surrounding one of the four partners in Belgium's centre-left coalition did not prevent the government from functioning properly. ($ = 34.91 Belgian Francs)
